title: Potential dividers
examples: How does changing the resistance affect the output voltage?
Can I use this circuit to measure something other than light?
What is the formula for calculating the output voltage?

explain.say: Today we are looking at potential dividers in circuits.
The ratio rule tells us how voltage splits across resistors.
For example, if the total resistance is ten ohms and the load is two ohms, the output voltage is one fifth of the input.
Sensors can be placed as the load resistor in these dividers.
A common application is using a photoresistor as a light sensor.
In real life, car headlights use a potential divider to measure light intensity.

faq.q: Does the load resistance affect the voltage reading?
faq.a: Yes, the load resistance is a crucial part of the calculation. A change in this resistance will change the output voltage significantly.
asks: How does the load affect the output?
Is the load resistance important for the ratio?

faq.q: Can I use this for anything other than light?
faq.a: Absolutely. You can use it with any sensor whose resistance changes predictably, like temperature sensors.
asks: What other sensors work in this setup?
Can I measure temperature this way?

faq.q: What is the formula for the output voltage?
faq.a: The output voltage is found by multiplying the input voltage by the ratio of the load resistance to the total resistance.
asks: Write down the voltage divider formula.

faq.q: What happens if the load resistance is very small?
faq.a: If the load resistance becomes very small, the output voltage will also become very small, approaching zero volts.
asks: What if Rload is near zero?
Does a tiny load cause low voltage?

faq.q: Is the sensor resistance always in series?
faq.a: Yes, for the basic potential divider setup, the sensor must be connected in series with the other resistors.
asks: Must the sensor be in line?

facts: The potential divider uses two or more resistors in series.
The output voltage is proportional to the ratio of resistances.
A photoresistor's resistance changes with the amount of light.
The formula is Vout = Vin (Rload / (R1 + Rload)).

quiz.say: If Vin is 12 volts, R1 is 10 ohms, and Rload is 5 ohms, what is Vout?
quiz.why: The output voltage is calculated using the ratio rule: 12 multiplied by five divided by fifteen equals four volts.

wrong.1: This assumes the voltage halves when the load is smaller than R1, which is incorrect.
wrong.2: This incorrectly adds the resistances together instead of using the ratio.
wrong.3: This incorrectly uses the ratio of the resistors rather than the voltage ratio.

quiz.say: If you want Vout to be exactly one third of Vin, what must the ratio Rload / Rtotal equal?
quiz.why: The ratio rule dictates that the output voltage is the input voltage multiplied by the required resistance ratio, so the ratio must be one third.

wrong.0: Multiplying the ratio by three would result in a voltage higher than the input voltage.
wrong.2: Squaring the ratio is not part of the standard potential divider formula.
wrong.3: Adding one to the ratio is incorrect; the ratio must be kept as a simple fraction.
